description:
We are Team Dust Devils, a group of students who love space, coding and engineering, supported by our teachers.

We named ourselves after the dust devils that swirl across Mars, which NASA’s rovers have photographed many times.

For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we built the 3D Mars Building Simulator to help plan a Mars base with real NASA data.

We shared the brainstorming, research, design and coding, and chose our team name by a vote.
summary: The Dust Devils' 3D Mars Building Simulator connects Martian site exploration with base design and preliminary mission planning. Users can explore map imagery, select a site, assemble a three-dimensional base, and investigate how terrain assumptions, materials, power, water, heating, mass, and cost affect a proposed mission. A route planner compares shortest, lower-hazard, energy-efficient, and balanced alternatives, while a guided workflow brings site, route, design, resource, and budget decisions into a mission report. NASA Mars Trek imagery and published Mars reference information provide context alongside explicitly labelled calculations and procedural models. The built-in route planner uses illustrative terrain; real-elevation routing requires an optional Python service and MOLA data. With English and Persian interfaces, the project addresses Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map by linking maps to the decisions they inform. It is an educational engineering workstation whose outputs are preliminary estimates, not certified designs or verified safe routes.
details:
Planning a Mars base means connecting terrain, construction, resources, and transport. A promising location may still demand difficult routes, additional power, heavier shielding, or a different structural design. We built 3D Mars Building Simulator to help users investigate these connected decisions in one interactive environment. Developed by The Dust Devils, a two-student team, the project addresses Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map by linking layered maps and location information to base design and route-planning studies.

The map can request NASA Mars Trek imagery, including MOLA colour relief and Viking MDIM imagery, with community-hosted OpenPlanetary alternatives. The final code also includes a CTX mosaic template and a configurable HiRISE option for selected sites. These higher-resolution sources depend on a working layer URL and actual coverage; the default HiRISE template must be supplied by the user. Layer-status indicators distinguish successfully loaded imagery from unverified or unavailable layers. A labelled procedural terrain model provides an illustrative alternative when imagery cannot be obtained.

Selecting a location opens a site profile with coordinates, elevation, estimated atmospheric conditions, and a simple buildability index. Approximate published MOLA elevations are included for a shortlist of landmarks; arbitrary locations otherwise use model estimates unless a data source or user override supplies an elevation. Pressure, temperature, sunlight, radiation, and ruggedness indicators are derived from simplified relations and assumptions. The interface distinguishes published values, calculations, assumptions, and synthetic terrain, helping users understand the evidence behind each result.

In the 3D engineering workstation, users can assemble a base and investigate the consequences of its layout, dimensions, and materials. The code includes structural screening, pressure and thermal checks for habitat walls, and estimates of electricity, battery storage, heating, water, mass, and construction and transport costs. These calculations share information about the selected site and proposed design. Cost scenarios are adjustable assumptions, rather than forecasts of the price of a real Mars mission.

The route planner compares four alternatives: shortest distance, lower modelled hazard exposure, lower estimated drive energy, and a weighted compromise. It presents elevation profiles and route metrics such as distance, ascent, maximum slope, estimated energy, and travel time, with CSV and GeoJSON export options. The built-in JavaScript solver uses procedural terrain and demonstrates optimisation rather than real traversability. A separate Python route service with a MOLA elevation dataset can provide a real-elevation pathway when installed and configured; the HTML file alone does not provide that service. Even with real elevation, grid-scale calculations cannot certify that a route is safe to drive.

A seven-step mission planner connects mission definition, site selection, route comparison, base design, resource checks, cost estimates, and reporting. The application includes mission-report export to PDF and HTML, bringing together the proposed design, calculations, data-source descriptions, assumptions, and limitations. Its creative contribution is this connected workflow: users can explore how changing one planning choice affects other parts of their mission, while keeping the status of the underlying information visible.

The application uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for three-dimensional graphics and cannon.js for illustrative rigid-body dynamics. It provides English and Persian interfaces. The optional route-service integration is described in the code as Python-based. Claude supported the project throughout research, implementation, explanations, and presentation preparation; Codex assisted only with reviewing the supplied materials and preparing this submission text.

The intended users are students, educators, and space enthusiasts who want to explore engineering trade-offs through a visual, hands-on activity. The simulator supports preliminary investigation and discussion. Model limitations remain explicit: terrain may be synthetic, several material properties and environmental inputs are placeholders or simplified estimates, and rigid-body animation is not a validated structural or fracture simulation. The project does not certify structures for flight or human occupancy. Operational use would require further data verification, experimental validation, and independent engineering review; these are development needs, not completed capabilities.

How to open the project: Download the HTML file from the Project link and open the downloaded file in a modern desktop browser. Internet access is needed to load external graphics libraries, web fonts, and live imagery; complete operation on a fresh offline browser is not established. The user manual is provided separately, with instructions and additional project context: Open the user manual. The demonstration video has its own Project Demonstration link.
